events.title: Franni Cash: Here I Am Tour 2026
events.description: For fans of We The Kingdom, Jamie MacDonald, and CAIN Franni Cash doesn’t just say what’s on her mind; she sings it as loudly as possible. The GRAMMY® Award-nominated Platinum singer, songwriter, and producer isn’t afraid to speak truth to power, tear down false idols, or point out hypocrisy when it comes to religion, church, or “Country Club Christians” —as she does on the likes of “Church Clothes” and “Koolaid. ” Opening up about her doubts, questions, and struggles in conversation, at shows, and on tape has made her faith stronger and given her music meaning. To paint a personal picture, she chooses to sonically color outside of the lines. The songstress spikes soulful-style hooks with rock ‘n’ roll attitude, bringing soul to Americana-style instrumentation, as she laces a sly sense of humor into the fabric of her unapologetic storytelling. She even co-opts and reclaims words and phrases once used to lambast her (such as “Jezebel”) for her own. Now, Franni declares who she is on her 2026 debut LP , Here I Am. She intentionally arranged and sequenced this 13-track body of work to tell her story in the order that she wanted to. Over the course of the journey, she looked back on how far she’s come. “I don’t know anybody who hasn’t had a problem with religion at some point, ” she observes. “Just because you’ve been burned by a church or by broken people in the church, it doesn’t mean you can’t have faith. To me, that’s what this record is about. It’s about coming back to music and true faith in a relationship with God, addressing the pain and ultimately seeking to heal from it. ” Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Gallery B Presents “Intersections | Realism & Abstraction”
events.description: “ INTERSECTIONS ⎸ Realism & Abstraction” is a group exhibition featuring four artists – Lawrence Chandler, Angela Iovino, Ariana Progri, and Ravi Raman – with distinct art styles in conversation with each other, showing that even the most realistic art is a form of abstraction (a reduction of reality) and that abstract art can hold elements of structural, grounded reality. Instead of treating realism and abstraction as binary opposites, works in the exhibition also intersect both worlds, showcasing how different artists navigate the spectrum between the two styles. Viewers not only will see realistic figures and recognizable subjects dissolving into, or emerging from abstract backgrounds, but also the use of bold brushstrokes, form, color, and textures to convey emotion rather than literal details.

Six albums and four Latin Grammy nominations later—including two Best Flamenco Album wins for Libres (2022) and Flamencas (2025)—the group continues to push the boundaries of flamenco, blending traditional Spanish folk–inspired guitar with pop and hip-hop influences. Founding member Marta Robles is joined by Paula Rodríguez, Laura Pacios, and Alicia Grillo, whose roots span Seville, Cataluña, La Mancha, and Galicia. Their sound draws on these regional traditions alongside Cuban rumba, while their songwriting centers a woman’s perspective. The group’s songs of liberation have earned them an international audience and strong connections within Spanish and Latin American LGBTQ+ communities.

events.description: What: Local authors' book launch and signing Where: The Barn at Honey's Harvest Farm (5801 Brooks Woods Road, Lothian MD 20711) When: Sunday November 8, 2026, 12pm-4pm Join author, speaker, and Chesapeake Bay advocate Mick Blackistone along with well-known award-winning artist Mitzi Bernard at Honey's Harvest Farm as they celebrate the launch of their book, Women Who Work the Waters of the Chesapeake Bay . "I wrote this book with Mitzi Bernard about the women who work the waters of the Chesapeake and her tributaries because, in my opinion, it was past due. Mitzi and I fell 'in love' with each and every one of them because of their persistence, determination, dedication and deep abiding love for working as watermen. They are young and old. Married and single. They wouldn’t stand out in a crowd unless you see them for who they are: Hunter Gatherers in the deepest sense. They live for family, community, and commercial fishing. They work as hard as any man and they sweat as much too. events.title: Monocacy Battlefield Tour
events.description: The Battle that Saved Washington Battlefields have a remarkable habit of looking peaceful. You’d never guess they were once full of people making spectacularly bad days for one another. On July 9, 1864, Monocacy National Battlefield became the setting for the battle remembered as the “Battle That Saved Washington.” By delaying the Confederate advance on the nation’s capital, the Union forces bought precious time for Washington’s defenses, making Monocacy one of the Civil War’s most significant, and perhaps most underestimated, battlefields. Beginning at the Monocacy Battlefield Visitor Center , we’ll journey through the battlefield with a National Park Service guide who brings the battlefield to life., following the course of the fighting while uncovering the stories of the soldiers who fought here and the families whose homes suddenly found themselves in the middle of history. With an expert guide bringing the landscape to life, you’ll discover how a quiet stretch of Maryland came to play an extraordinary role in the nation’s story. History happened here in a single day. The consequences took rather longer. DURATION: 1 hour DEPARTS FROM: Monocacy National Battlefield, 5201 Urbana Pike Frederick, MD 21704 TICKETING DETAILS: $35 per person. A minimum total of 15 tickets must be sold for the tour to run. If we don’t sell the required minimum of tickets, we’ll gladly refund your purchase or credit it toward another exciting tour. We’re committed to ensuring you have a fantastic experience, and we appreciate your understanding as we work to create fun, unforgettable events together!

events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. events.title: Rockville Musical Theatre presents “Caroline, or Change”
events.description: 8 performances | Oct. 31 and Nov. 6*, 7, 13 & 14 at 7:30 p.m. | Nov. 1, 8 & 15 at 2 p.m. Set in one of the most pivotal times in America’s history, the Tony-nominated Caroline, or Change is riveting, moving, and awe-inspiring. Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four, working in a service job for a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child, but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. Caroline, or Change, produces a valuable theatrical experience that continues to thrill audiences the world over. It is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. events.description: What Do the 2026 Midterm Elections Mean for America’s Political Future? Please join the AAUW McLean Area Branch for a special presentation by Stephen Farnsworth, PhD, Professor Emeritus of Political Science and International Affairs at the University of Mary Washington. Dr. Farnsworth will unpack the election results and will examine what they reveal about public opinion, the balance of power in Congress, and the future of the president’s policy agenda. Drawing on his expertise in American politics, presidential leadership, political communication, and Virginia politics, Dr. Farnsworth will explore how election outcomes may reshape relations between the White House and Congress, influence national policy debates, and set the stage for the 2028 presidential election. events.title: "Inside Gaza" Film Screening & Discussion
events.description: The Institute for Middle East Studies is proud to announce a screening of the award winning documentary Inside Gaza, followed by remarks from film director Hélène Lam Trong and featured journalist Mai Yaghi. Since the Hamas attack on 7 October 2023 and the Israeli reprisals that followed, international journalists and media have no access to the Gaza Strip. Agence France-Presse journalists, who were permanently stationed in Gaza, were among the last independent witnesses to the abuses committed in the hellscape that Gaza has become. Featuring previously unseen footage and testimony from reporters Mai Yaghi and Adel Zaanoun, as well as photojournalists Mahmud Hams and Mohammed Abed, Inside Gaza delivers a powerful account of conditions on the ground, underscoring the vital importance of a free and independent press. All are invited to join the Institute for Middle East Studies for this film screening and discussion with film director Hélène Lam Trong and featured journalist Mai Yaghi. A trailer for the documentary can be found here. Speakers: Hélène Lam Trong is a French documentary filmmaker. Her 2023 documentary Daech, les enfants fantômes (ISIS, the Ghost Children) earned her the Albert Londres Prize for an audio-visual work. Independent since 2018, she worked for several years at Radio France then at France télévisions. In 2024, she directed Raqqa, l'ombre de Daech. Mai Yaghi is an Agence France-Presse (AFP) journalist and one of the protagonists of Inside Gaza. Ms. Yaghi

events.title: Beyond Discovery: Archaeology, Heritage and Partnership in the Galilee
events.description: Join the CCAS Department of Classical and Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations for a presentation on the U.S.-funded Galilee Heritage Project at Huqoq and Bethsaida. Focusing primarily on Huqoq, this lecture traces the journey from archaeological discovery to conservation, interpretation and public engagement, including new finds from 2026, the Secrets of Huqoq exhibition and new digital initiatives. Speaker: Dr. Shua Kisilevitz, Albright Institute of Archaeological Research and Tel Aviv University About the Project: What happens to an archaeological site after excavation ends, but long before it can open to the public? The Galilee Heritage Project addresses this challenge at two recently excavated sites near the Sea of Galilee, the late Roman synagogue and extraordinary mosaics of Huqoq and the Byzantine church at Bethsaida (El-Araj), identified by its excavators as the Church of the Apostles. Together, these exceptional discoveries offer compelling windows into the culturally and religiously diverse world of the Galilee in Late Antiquity. Led by the W. F. Albright Institute of Archaeological Research with U.S. federal support, the project also highlights the enduring role of American scholarship and American-Israeli institutional partnership in researching, preserving and sharing the region's archaeological heritage.

events.title: Book Seminar - Capitalism in South Korea, 1945-2025
events.description: How did South Korea’s rapid economic transformation shape its democracy, institutions, and society? In his book, Keun Lee examines South Korea’s development since 1945 through a framework of compressed development, decompression, and convergence. He explores how rapid growth helped create a middle class that demanded political freedom, and how IMF-led reforms following the Asian financial crisis reshaped the country’s economic trajectory. The seminar will examine the book's findings. Read a full abstract here. About the Speaker Keun Lee is a Distinguished Professor of Economics at Chung-Ang University and professor emeritus at Seoul National University. He is a fellow at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, founding director of the Center for Economic Catch-Up, and an editor of Research Policy. He obtained his PhD in economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Lee spent a year at the World Bank as a visiting scholar in 2004 and 2005, received the 2014 Schumpeter Prize for Schumpeterian Analysis of Economic Catch-up and served as vice-chairman of South Korea’s National Economic Advisory Council in 2021. His recent books include China’s Technological Leapfrogging and Economic Catch-up (2021) and Innovation–Development Detours for Latecomers (2024). Hosted by the Elliott School’s International Science and Technology Policy program, with co-sponsorship from the GW Institute for Korean Studies.

events.title: Franni Cash: Here I Am Tour 2026
events.description: For fans of We The Kingdom, Jamie MacDonald, and CAIN Franni Cash doesn’t just say what’s on her mind; she sings it as loudly as possible. To paint a personal picture, she chooses to sonically color outside of the lines. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: Rick Steves
events.description: In the 1970s, the ultimate trip for any backpacker was the storied “Hippie Trail,” a 3,000-mile trek from Istanbul to Kathmandu. A 23-year-old Rick Steves made the trek in 1978, and like a travel writer in training, he documented everything along the way: jumping off a moving train, making friends in Tehran, getting lost in Lahore, getting high for the first time in Herat, battling leeches in Pokhara, and more. The experience ignited his love of travel and forever broadened his perspective on the world. On the Hippie Trail: Istanbul to Kathmandu and the Making of a Travel Writer —a New York Times bestseller now out in paperback—contains edited selections from Rick Steves’ journal and travel photos with a 45-years-later preface and postscript reflecting on how his journey through Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, and Nepal changed his life.

events.title: A Virtual Lecture from Historic Annapolis – William and Dinah Nuthead: Maryland’s First Printers
events.description: Before Jonas and Anne Catharine Hoof Green, there was William and Dinah Nuthead, Maryland’s first printing duo. William Nuthead was the first printer in Maryland and the first to operate a press in Virginia, establishing his business in St. Mary’s City in 1685 after being barred from printing in Virginia by the colonial government. Following his death in 1695, his widow Dinah Nuthead took over the business and became the first licensed female printer in the American colonies. Join Rod Cofield as he discusses his research into their lives that led to his Maryland Historical Magazine article, “Much Ado about Nuthead.” The Historic Annapolis Virtual Lecture Series is offered free of charge thanks to the generosity of an anonymous donor. If you enjoy this program, we hope you will consider becoming a member or making a donation today to support Historic Annapolis and our mission to connect all people with our shared history. Can’t watch live? All lectures will be recorded. Please register and you’ll receive the link to watch the recording after the event. Advance registration required; registration closes on half-hour prior to lecture. Cost: FREE This lecture will be offered virtually by Zoom. Upon registration, you will be sent the link for the video conference to join on the evening of the lecture. If you do not receive your confirmation email after you register, please check your Spam folder, or email Cara Garside at cara.garside@annapolis.org . To learn more about Zoom and to download the app to your computer, visit the Zoom website . About Our Presenter: Rod Cofield is the Executive Director at Jefferson Patterson Park and Museum in Calvert County. He was previously the Executive Director at Historic London Town and Gardens in Edgewater, Maryland. In recent years, ABT Studio Company has performed in such international destinations as the United Kingdom, Greece, South Korea, the Philippines, Hong Kong, and Mexico and at a wide variety of US performing arts centers, universities, festivals, and galas. ABT Studio Company dancers perform favorite excerpts from the classical and neoclassical canons alongside inventive contemporary pieces, commissioning today’s brightest choreographers to create new ballets on the dancers each season. Performances feature a wide variety of styles, offering something for everyone to enjoy—from ballet newcomers to lifelong fans!

events.title: Book Talk- Caring Like a State: The Politics of Russia's Demographic Crisis
events.description: The post-Soviet Russian state has long been haunted by the specter of a dwindling population. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, and despite well-publicized pro-natalist campaigns, the population has continued to contract, raising doubts about the state’s capacity to care effectively for its citizens. The talk draws on Inna Leykin's book Caring Like a State: The Politics of Russia's Demographic Crisis that explores the national preoccupation with demography from the dissolution of the Soviet Union to the full-scale invasion of sovereign Ukraine. Moving beyond policy analysis, it focuses on the role of socio-demographic knowledge in shaping how the state defines social problems, identifies target populations, and determines who should be the object of state care and intervention. By tracing the circulation of demographic knowledge across expert communities, state institutions, and everyday life, the book shows how the “demographic crisis” has been socially organized and how responses to it generate alternative understandings and practices of care that do not always align with state visions. The discussion will be moderated by Ivan Grek, Director of the Russia Program.

events.title: Forgiveness: Grace in the Messiness of Being Human
events.description: Forgiveness is far more complicated than a simple spiritual decision. Drawing on theology, psychology, and physical well-being, this Taproom Theology conversation explores the grace we receive and the forgiveness we extend, while making room for the anger, grief, regret, and unresolved hurt that shape our lives and relationships. Together, we’ll wrestle with the tensions between grace and accountability, forgiveness and boundaries, and healing and reconciliation. We’ll consider why forgiveness doesn’t mean excusing harm, forgetting what happened, or returning to unsafe relationships, and how God’s love meets us not just when we forgive, but throughout the messy, imperfect process of getting there. Join Taproom Theology for an insightful evening featuring Sage Bolte, PhD, a renowned educator and mental health therapist. Explore the complex themes of grace and forgiveness within a relaxed atmosphere where beliefs are brewed and hope is on tap.

events.title: Life of Courage: Bruce McCandless and the Pacific War
events.venue: U.S. Naval Institute's Jack C. Taylor Conference Center
events.description: Join the U.S. Naval Institute on 10 November 2026 at 10:30 AM ET at the Jack C. Taylor Conference Center, in Annapolis, MD for a look inside the new book Iron and Fire: The Pacific War Story of Destroyer Captain Bruce McCandless with Bruce McCandless III as he recounts his grandfather’s—Admiral Bruce McCandless—wartime experiences across the Pacific. Lieutenant Bruce McCandless was at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, fought aboard the heavy cruiser USS San Francisco (CA 38) through the brutal Guadalcanal campaign. Later promoted to captain, he commanded the destroyer USS Gregory (DD 802) during the final drive across the Pacific. Late in life, retiring as an admiral, he dictated his wartime memories to his daughter Sue; the manuscript was then set aside for many years. Iron and Fire draws on family letters, photographs, shipmates’ recollections, and stories passed down through generations to share his story. Registration and other Information: All in-person guests must register by 25 September 2026. Due to the requirements of the U.S. Naval Academy and the timing of this event, in person attendance is only open to U.S. citizens. The conference will take place at the U.S. Naval Institute's Jack C. Taylor Conference Center, which is located on the grounds of the U.S. Naval Academy. A limited amount of parking is available at the Jack C. Taylor Conference Center. We welcome our audience in-person and via live-stream on the U.S. Naval Institute’s YouTube Channel.

events.title: Ted Scheinman for Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness
events.description: Growing up in a hyper-educated, artistic, eccentric family, Ted Scheinman, the son of a medical doctor and an English professor, spent much of his precocious childhood as a writer and performer—and his greatest performance was as someone who was happy. He recognized his depression early and recorded its effects in a series of tragicomic journals, always hoping that the ritual of doing so would palliate if not cure. While the clouds occasionally parted, particularly during Ted’s years of intellectual questing at Hotchkiss and Yale—and, fleetingly, through his emergence as a successful journalist—his gloom kept returning, seemingly more debilitating each time. Eventually, a series of emotional plunges deposited Ted, at age thirty-five, in a psych ward in Washington, DC. There, he began an intensive course of electroconvulsive therapy—considered by most a treatment of last resort. The controversial procedure saved his life, but it also exacted a price: he was now missing important pieces of his memory. By turns deeply gripping, startlingly perceptive, understatedly hilarious, and heartbreakingly poignant, particularly in Ted’s depiction of his romantic relationships, Jolt asks: How do our families shape who we are, for good and ill? How much of our character is ingrained versus sculpted by circumstances? How can we adapt when our memory fails? Perhaps most critically: What are we willing to sacrifice to have a chance at life? events.title: Virtual Lecture – William and Dinah Nuthead: Maryland’s First Printers
events.description: Before Jonas and Anne Catharine Hoof Green, there was William and Dinah Nuthead, Maryland’s first printing duo. William Nuthead was the first printer in Maryland and the first to operate a press in Virginia, establishing his business in St. Mary’s City in 1685 after being barred from printing in Virginia by the colonial government. Following his death in 1695, his widow Dinah Nuthead took over the business and became the first licensed female printer in the American colonies. Join Rod Cofield as he discusses his research into their lives that led to his Maryland Historical Magazine article, “Much Ado about Nuthead.” The Historic Annapolis Virtual Lecture Series is offered free of charge thanks to the generosity of an anonymous donor. If you enjoy this program, we hope you will consider becoming a member or making a donation today to support Historic Annapolis and our mission to connect all people with our shared history. Can’t watch live? All lectures will be recorded. Please register and you’ll receive the link to watch the recording after the event. Advance registration required; registration closes on half-hour prior to lecture. Cost: FREE

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Israel’s Existential Election: A Conversation with Dr. Dahlia Scheindlin
events.description: On October 27th, Israeli citizens went to the polls for the first time since the October 7th, 2023 Hamas attack and the years of war that have followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Dr. Dahlia Scheindlin, Israel's foremost public opinion expert, will analyze the complex results of this fateful election and their implications for Israel, conflict with the Palestinians, relations with the US and regional politics. The Elliott School's Ned Lazarus will moderate. Dr. Dahlia Scheindlin is a public opinion expert and political strategist who has advised national campaigns in Israel and fifteen other countries. Dahlia is a Senior Analyst and columnist for Haaretz. Her book, The Crooked Timber of Democracy in Israel: Promise Unfulfilled was listed on Foreign Affairs' Best Books of 2024. Dahlia conducts extensive public opinion research for civil society organizations, including joint Israeli-Palestinian surveys. Her writing has appeared in The New York Times, The Guardian, The Observer, Foreign Affairs, Foreign Policy, Financial Times, Time Magazine, The New York Review of Books, The New Statesman, and The New York Post. Dr. Ned Lazarus is Teaching Associate Professor of International Affairs at the Elliott School and an Israel Institute Teaching Fellow. A Conflict Resolution scholar, practitioner and evaluator, Ned has conducted evaluative studies of peacebuilding initiatives on behalf of USAID, USIP, the European Union and the US Department of State. events.title: Korea Policy Forum- Recalibrating Northeast Asian Geopolitics after the U.S. Midterms
events.description: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections will set the political landscape in Washington for the remainder of President Trump’s second term, with important implications for U.S. policy toward Northeast Asia. At the same time, shifting U.S.–China relations, developments on the Korean Peninsula, and growing economic and technological competition are adding new uncertainties to the regional order. This Korea Policy Forum brings together leading experts from the United States and South Korea to assess the post-midterm outlook for Northeast Asia from both Washington and Seoul perspectives. Following a keynote address on South Korea’s strategic choices, the discussion will examine regional security, the U.S.–ROK alliance, U.S.–China relations, and emerging challenges in trade, technology, and economic security. The GW Institute for Korean Studies invites you to join this timely and forward-looking discussion.

events.title: LeVar Burton
events.description: Tracing the different eras of his life—from “Roots” to “Star Trek: The Next Generation” to “Reading Rainbow” and far beyond the camera—actor LeVar Burton fearlessly opens up about growing up during the Civil Rights Movement, being raised by a remarkable mother, and discovering his calling as a storyteller in Take My Word for It. He explores how acting has served as both a source of transformation and an escape from the most difficult parts of his past, while also confronting the challenges of being a parent, husband, and householder. As Burton honors the loved ones whose strength and resilience shaped him, he also asks what we owe to our ancestors and to each other, reflecting on the deep necessity he’s always felt to advocate for liberation and equity. Burton will be in conversation with Michele Norris, a Peabody and Emmy Award-winning journalist, the host of the podcast “ Your Mama’s Kitchen,” and the author of Our Hidden Conversations: What Americans Really Think About Race and Identity.

Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. Art Capital: Museum Politics and the Making of the Louvre Abu Dhabi
events.description: Attend In-Person or Attend Online The Institute for Middle East Studies, in-partnership with the Corcoran School of the Arts and Design, invites you to join author Beth Derderian and discussant Joshua Bell for an exploration of Art Capital: Museum Politics and the Making of the Louvre Abu Dhabi. Museums often served nationalist and imperialist interests in the past, but the primary force in the 21st century is the market. Museum franchising—exemplified by the Louvre Abu Dhabi—is one of the most visible cases of the increasing entanglement of art and museums with capital interests. Such projects are often touted as global enterprises diversifying the art world. Frequently, critics of these controversial projects question these claims and market influence. The intersection of these two forces—increasing capitalization and moving toward inclusivity—creates a fundamental tension, and that is the subject of Beth Derderian's Art Capital. Focusing on the decade between the Louvre Abu Dhabi's announcement and its eventual opening, the book analyzes how major shifts away from the 19th- and 20th-century paradigm of culture-state representation play out in museums' and artists' everyday practices. Dr. Derderian traces the emergence of a new logic, wherein the ways that artists represent the state shift, as does the notion of what constitutes 'good art.' events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. events.title: Giles Corey
events.description: First released in 2011, the self-titled Giles Corey album began with a simple constraint: acoustic instruments only. That boundary opened into something much larger—guitar, piano, ghostly choirs, heavy organ, field recordings, and sudden walls of sound arranged around an intimate singer-songwriter core. The songs move through depression, death, history, and the paranormal without treating any of them as distant ideas. Quiet desperation gives way to cathartic outburst; private confession becomes communal release. The album and its accompanying book have since gathered a fervent following, often described by listeners in the language of ritual or religious experience. events.title: Mental Reset: Sound Bath + Reiki : Thursday Evenings in Falls Church
events.address: 7777 Leesburg Pike, Ste 204S, Falls Church, VA 22043
events.description: Thursday is a weird day. The week isn't over, but you are. Mental Reset is one hour at the end of the workday where nobody needs anything from you. You come in, you lie down on a mat, you get a blanket and a bolster, and for the next sixty minutes your only job is to listen. I play crystal singing bowls, guide you through a short meditation so your mind has something to do besides replay the day, and offer Reiki while you rest. Most people tell me some version of the same thing afterward: the noise in their head finally turned down. Not off: down. Enough that they can go home and actually be home, instead of answering emails in their head at the dinner table. You don't need experience. You don't need to know how to meditate, and you definitely don't need to “clear your mind.” If you could do that, you wouldn't need this class. First-timers are in the room most weeks. There are ten spots. That's deliberate. It's a small room, I can see everyone in it, and it never feels like an event. It feels like an exhale. A few regulars started as skeptics; more than one of our Google reviews comes from someone who arrived doubting the whole thing and left surprised at how settled they felt. You don't have to believe in anything for an hour of sound and rest to do you some good. Run by Victoria Vita: CPA for 20+ years, healer for 7+. I sat behind a desk with a brain that wouldn't switch off for a long time before I found this work. Thursday nights are built for the person I used to be. Rated 5.0 from 32 Google reviews. Come straight from work. Leave like the week let go of you first. What's included: • 60 minutes of crystal singing bowls, guided meditation and Reiki • Mat, blanket, and bolster everything is here; you bring nothing • Small group: 10 people maximum, same teacher every week • Time at the end to sit up slowly, have water, and not rush out Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. events.title: North Africa 1942: Torch
events.description: On November 8, 1942, Allied forces launched Operation Torch, the first major joint Allied operation of World War II. The landings in North Africa marked a turning point in the war and helped build momentum for the Allied campaign. Just days later, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill declared, “This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. events.title: Religion in Asia: Women's Rights and Religious Conversion Laws in India
events.description: In India, Hindu nationalists are curtailing women's rights through accusations that Muslim men are engaged in "love jihad"--a conspiracy to convert women into Muslims by seduction. The new laws in various Indian states penalize interfaith marriage between Muslims or Christians and Hindus. Some states require notifying the government of religious conversion 60 to 90 days in advance. Other regulations assume that marriage with a woman or minority community member who has converted is under coercion. These laws allow family members to file complaints about voluntary marriages, leading to arrests and government harassment. These laws assume that women have no agency and are only involved in interfaith marriage because they have been manipulated. Many families are willing to use the new laws to stop their daughters from entering a marriage that hasn't been family approved. This discussion will look at the new laws and how they are being implemented to restrict women's rights in India.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: The Maryland 1864 Constitution: A Border State’s Soldiers Stand for Freedom
events.description: Join Peerless Rockville as we mark Maryland Emancipation Day and Veterans Day with psychiatrist and author Dr. Stephen A. Goldman. In this presentation, he will discuss the 1864 Maryland Constitutional Election that emancipated enslaved Marylanders, the only state in the Union to end slavery through the state consititution. The soldiers’ vote in Maryland would greatly determine the state’s future, and their overwhelming support for slavery’s abolition exemplified how the war radicalized so many white servicemen throughout the Union. Of all the states involved in the Civil War, Maryland epitomized its harsh “brother against brother” reality, and the complicated prewar circumstances of slavery and freedom. While a border slave state, Maryland remained in the Union, and contributed 63,000 soldiers, sailors, and marines to its war effort, including ten thousand African Americans. By 1864, the state had reached a crossroads that the entire nation was confronting – a Civil War that had turned savage, whether Abraham Lincoln would be re-elected, and what would be the fate of four million human beings held in bondage. On November 1, 1864, the Maryland electorate voted to end slavery in the state. ABOUT THE SPEAKER Stephen A. Goldman, M.D. is a Distinguished Life Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association, war historian, and the only physician to serve on the Abraham Lincoln Institute Board of Directors. events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.description: Virginia helped shape the beginnings of our nation, and local audiences can experience the drama, humor and music behind America’s founding in 1776 , the Tony Award-winning musical presented by The Pickwick Players. Just in time for America’s 250th anniversary, 1776 takes audiences inside the Continental Congress, where John Adams pushes for independence, Benjamin Franklin brings his wit and wisdom, and Virginia’s own Thomas Jefferson is called upon to put the revolutionary cause into words. events.title: 25th Annual Jazz4Justice
events.description: Join us as we celebrate the 25th Anniversary of Jazz4Justice™, an award-winning partnership between the George Mason University Jazz Program and Northern Virginia's legal community. For a quarter century, Jazz4Justice has demonstrated the power of music to unite communities, raise awareness of the justice gap, and support access to civil legal services for those who cannot afford an attorney. Recognized by the legal profession and honored with George Mason University's Jack Wood Award for Town-Gown Collaboration, Jazz4Justice has become a model for meaningful community engagement. In partnership with Legal Services of Northern Virginia, proceeds from this concert help provide free civil legal assistance to low-income individuals and families facing issues such as housing, domestic violence, consumer protection, family law, veterans' services, and public benefits. Through volunteer attorneys and dedicated legal advocates, LSNV works every day to help ensure that justice is not determined by one's ability to pay. The evening will feature the George Mason Jazz Program performing swinging classics from the golden age of the big band, celebrating both the enduring spirit of jazz and the remarkable partnership that has helped strengthen our community for twenty-five years.

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.description: Take a student-led tour of the exhibitions currently on view at the Brady Art Gallery: "Unfossilizing African Art" and "Cracks and Reforms". Unfossilizing African Art recontextualizes African material culture objects that have been held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students across four seminar courses conducted original research to deepen understanding of the collection and reconsider how these objects are interpreted and exhibited. Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection examines a decade shaped by political upheaval, social transformation, migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition. This exhibition, developed as part of an art history class taught by Associate Professor Bibi Obler, is accompanied by a catalog designed by graphic design students.

events.title: Camelot
events.description: Welcome to CAMELOT! Borrowing from the Arthurian legends, CAMELOT is Lerner and Loewe's fantastical masterpiece. An idealistic King Arthur hopes to create a kingdom built on honor and dignity, embodied by his Knights of The Round Table. He establishes an order built on using “might for right.” His ideals, however, are tested when his lovely queen, Guenevere, falls in love with his most loyal knight, Lancelot. Add in the dastardly Mordred and his wicked schemes and it soon appears this dream of a kingdom may only exist for one brief, shining moment. ​ This stirring Golden Age musical has enchanted generations of theatregoers with its sweeping score and iconic characters. It is a romance, a tragedy, a comedy, an adventure, a fantasy, and a stirring exploration of power and leadership all at once. And above all, it is a piece about the stories and ideals we pass along to future generations.​

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Caroline, or Change the Musical
events.description: 8 performances | October 31 and November 6*, 7, 13, and 14 at 7:30pm | November 1, 8, and 15 at 2:00pm *Friday, November 6 will include ASL interpretation and free tickets for Montgomery County residents! Full information at www.r-m-t.org/caroline-or-change Set in one of the most pivotal times in America’s history, the Tony-nominated Caroline, or Change is riveting, moving and awe-inspiring. Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. ​ In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four working in a service job to a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. ​ Caroline, or Change is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. It is a story that will open minds. It is a story that will change theatergoers

events.title: Charlie Parr
events.description: Charlie Parr, a Duluth-based guitarist and folk troubadour, delivers what Rolling Stone calls "a gritty blend of Delta blues and Depression-era roots music soaked in his hardscrabble voice," and NPR praises as "expertly picked resonator guitar and lyrics that puncture the soul." Over two-and-a-half decades, Parr has released twenty albums while performing up to 275 shows a year at tastemaker events like Newport Folk Fest and Pickathon. A continuer of folk tradition, Parr's sound draws from Folkways legends like Lead Belly and Woody Guthrie, imbued with blues and folk echoes of decades past. His music is shaped by his working-class Minnesota upbringing and Depression-era stories from his father. His 2021 Smithsonian Folkways debut Last of the Better Days Ahead foregrounded his lyrical craftsmanship and bluesman confidence with spare production elevating his blues poetry. His 2024 release Little Sun wove together stories celebrating music, community, and nature into an ambitious, raw album exemplifying his blend of blues and folk traditions with poetic originality. His 2026 album Rooming House joins the chorus of WPA-era socially conscious folk operas and outlaw country concept albums, poignantly allegorizing his experiences and those around him. Jammin' Java welcomes him to Fairfax County, Virginia.

The Duluth-based guitarist, songwriter, and interpreter of traditional music has released twenty albums over two-and-a-half decades and has been known to perform up to 275 shows a year. The sounds from his working-class upbringing—including Folkways legends such as Lead Belly and Woody Guthrie—imbue Parr’s music with stylistic echoes of blues and folk icons of decades past. Parr sees himself merely as a continuer of a folk tradition. events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Gallery B Presents “Intersections | Realism & Abstraction”
events.description: “ INTERSECTIONS ⎸ Realism & Abstraction” is a group exhibition featuring four artists – Lawrence Chandler, Angela Iovino, Ariana Progri, and Ravi Raman – with distinct art styles in conversation with each other, showing that even the most realistic art is a form of abstraction (a reduction of reality) and that abstract art can hold elements of structural, grounded reality. Instead of treating realism and abstraction as binary opposites, works in the exhibition also intersect both worlds, showcasing how different artists navigate the spectrum between the two styles. Viewers not only will see realistic figures and recognizable subjects dissolving into, or emerging from abstract backgrounds, but also the use of bold brushstrokes, form, color, and textures to convey emotion rather than literal details.

events.description: Join us as we celebrate the 25th Anniversary of Jazz4Justice™, an award-winning partnership between the George Mason University Jazz Program and Northern Virginia's legal community. For a quarter century, Jazz4Justice has demonstrated the power of music to unite communities, raise awareness of the justice gap, and support access to civil legal services for those who cannot afford an attorney. Recognized by the legal profession and honored with George Mason University's Jack Wood Award for Town-Gown Collaboration, Jazz4Justice has become a model for meaningful community engagement. In partnership with Legal Services of Northern Virginia, proceeds from this concert help provide free civil legal assistance to low-income individuals and families facing issues such as housing, domestic violence, consumer protection, family law, veterans' services, and public benefits. Through volunteer attorneys and dedicated legal advocates, LSNV works every day to help ensure that justice is not determined by one's ability to pay. The evening will feature the George Mason Jazz Program performing swinging classics from the golden age of the big band, celebrating both the enduring spirit of jazz and the remarkable partnership that has helped strengthen our community for twenty-five years. events.description: 5:00pm • Suggested $10 - $20 donation JM Stevens Austin-based singer-songwriter JM Stevens brings a lifetime of road-worn stories, memorable melodies, and unvarnished honesty to the stage. A former frontman of the longtime SXSW favorite Moonlight Towers, Stevens has built a powerful solo catalog rooted in thoughtful songwriting, acoustic guitar, harmonica, and a voice that feels equally at home in a quiet listening room or a late-night roadhouse. His latest album, Wish on a River Bridge, is a stripped-down and deeply personal collection shaped by the miles between shows. Recorded largely by Stevens at East Austin Recording, the album finds him exploring old beginnings, fresh starts, and all the uncertain territory in between. With echoes of heartland rock, folk, and American roots music, the songs favor emotional truth over ornament—leaving nowhere to hide and plenty to feel. Released in March 2025 on Stevens’ own Crosstie Records, Wish on a River Bridge takes its title from a childhood family tradition: holding your breath and making a wish while crossing a bridge. events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four, working in a service job for a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child, but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. Caroline, or Change, produces a valuable theatrical experience that continues to thrill audiences the world over. It is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. events.description: Virginia helped shape the beginnings of our nation, and local audiences can experience the drama, humor and music behind America’s founding in 1776 , the Tony Award-winning musical presented by The Pickwick Players. Just in time for America’s 250th anniversary, 1776 takes audiences inside the Continental Congress, where John Adams pushes for independence, Benjamin Franklin brings his wit and wisdom, and Virginia’s own Thomas Jefferson is called upon to put the revolutionary cause into words. The story also features Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, whose resolution calling for independence helped move the colonies toward a historic decision. What happens when a room full of passionate, stubborn and politically divided men try to agree on the future of a nation? There’s plenty of debate, a little scheming, larger-than-life personalities and some unforgettable music. With music and lyrics by Sherman Edwards and a book by Peter Stone, 1776 combines clever dialogue, colorful characters, political maneuvering and a memorable score. From the spirited opening number, “Sit Down, John,” to the lively “The Lees of Old Virginia” and the stirring “Is Anybody There?,” the music captures the humor, frustrations and high stakes behind the birth of a nation. Forget the dusty history books. 1776 presents the founding fathers as real people, with big egos, strong opinions, competing interests and a monumental decision to make. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. Over more than two decades of relentless grassroots touring, Adam Ezra Group has built something far bigger than a typical touring band: a fiercely independent, fan-powered community that expands one show at a time. Rooms across the country sell out when Adam Ezra Group comes to town, with longtime fans regularly traveling across state lines to catch multiple shows, drawn by the band's deep sense of community and the promise that no two nights are ever the same. The band never performs from a fixed setlist; instead, they shape each night around the energy in the room. Songs, stories, and moments unfold in real time—part concert, part revival, and part reminder of what live music can still be at its best. Blending folk/Americana soul, rock 'n' roll energy, and deeply human songwriting, Adam Ezra Group has built one of the most authentic underground followings in live music today while quickly becoming recognized on a national level. SPIN describes them as "an independent underground folk band blowing up without selling out," a rise powered entirely by word of mouth, community activism, and genuine connection between band and audience that turns first-time listeners into lifelong fans. Catch them now while they're still playing intimate rooms where you can give Adam a hug on your way out. If you have limited motion in a joint(s), need an assistive device or have no physical complaints and want to stay that way, this talk is for you. We will address the strategies on how to do this with flare. Wear comfortable shoes and clothes you can move freely in. Dr. Patrice Winter, PT, DPT, MHA, FAAOMPT, is a retired professor from George Mason University’s College of Public Health, Department of Global and Community Health, where she taught health-related curriculum with emphasis in public health, disease, healthy living and aging well. Dr. Winter practiced physical therapy for over 35 years and was a spokesperson for the American Physical Therapy Association for almost twenty years.

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. From savory quiche to decadent chocolate tartlets, discover how the right wine can elevate every bite. ​Pairing Menu Almond Frangipane Tartlet with Apricot Preserves Paired with Cupola 2025 — Sauvignon Blanc & Sauvignon Gris Butternut Squash Quiche Paired with Rosé 2025 Virginia Country Ham Quiche Paired with Trellis 2021 — Red Blend Dark Chocolate Ganache Tartlet with Raspberry Jam Paired with Topiary 2023 — Red Blend Your experience also includes a Boxwood Gift Bag featuring a half bottle of wine, the perfect way to continue the celebration at home. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.
